newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ sees NZ$2.49 bln budget surplus in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: NZ sees NZ$2.49 bln budget surplus in 1996/97.

text.p: New Zealand Treasury on Monday released fresh projections showing the government would have a 1996/97 budget surplus of NZ$2.493 billion in the year to June 30, 1997, 2.6 percent of GDP.

The forecast is lower than the previous forecast released in September of $2.866 billion, 3.1 percent of GDP, and compares with the May budget forecast of a NZ$2.758 billion surplus, 2.9 percent of GDP.

In the new projections prepared as part of the December Economic and Fiscal Update, the surplus is projected to rise to $3.125 billion in 1997/98, $4.405 billion in 1998/99 and $6.107 billion in in 1999/00, or 5.5 percent of GDP.
The September forecasts projected surpluses of $3.388 billion in 1997/98, $4.703 billion in 1998/99 and $6.415 billion in 1999/00, or 5.9 percent of GDP.
Budget projections were for surpluses of NZ$3.29 billion in 1997/98 and $4.92 billion in 1998/99.
The projections include government decisions taken up to early November and assume no policy change.

But policies are expected to change with political parties in the final stages of coalition talks following the October 12 election. Economists predict that even if the New Zealand First Party, holding the balance of power, sides with the conservative ruling National Party, spending will increase sharply.
If it chooses the left-of-centre Labour Party, spending is expected to increase even more sharply.
Caretaker Finance Minister Bill Birch said the fiscal position remained strong because of high growth and responsible management.
Net public debt had fallen to 31.6 percent of GDP in the year to June 1996 from 52.8 percent in 1991/92. It was projected to fall below 14 percent of GDP by 1999/00.
Birch said the lower forecast operating surplus in the year to June 1997, followed by a modest rise the next year, was mainly due to the introduction of the Tax Reduction and Social Policy Programme.

Operating surpluses rising from 1996/97 reflected growth in revenue and flat expenses, as increases in education, health and social welfare spending were offset by reductions in finance costs. -- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
